Now the opening play answers itself. With 1:41 left the game was past the two-minute warning, so the
coach couldn't challenge (had he thrown the flag, he'd have lost a timeout for nothing). The replay
official in the stadium started the review, someone in New York decided it, and the referee only announced
it. And "control with both feet down in bounds" is two of the three gates of the catch rule, which is next.

### What actually gets reviewed

Play-by-play data records a review whenever one changes or stops the game, with the ruling that was
reviewed and the result, so you can see where replay earns its keep.

```{python}
#| label: fig-reviews
#| fig-cap: "The twelve rulings reviewed most often, 2021–2025 (regular season and playoffs), split by who asked: a coach's challenge (orange) or the booth (blue). The label gives the share of those reviews that reversed the call. Catch or no catch is by far the busiest question. Don't read the reversal rates as 'officials are usually wrong': every bar is a selected sample. Coaches challenge only when their staff has seen a replay that looks wrong, and the play-by-play generally records a booth review only when it stopped the game, not the routine quick confirmations of every touchdown, so both kinds of review are weighted toward close calls. Source: nflverse play-by-play (the review text in each play's description)."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.9))
ys = np.arange(len(tab))
ax.barh(ys, tab["challenge"], color=style.DEFENSE, height=0.62, label="Coach's challenge")
ax.barh(ys, tab["booth"], left=tab["challenge"], color=style.OFFENSE, height=0.62, label="Booth review")
for y, (_, row) in zip(ys, tab.iterrows()):
    ax.text(row.n + 6, y, f"{100 * row.rev:.0f}% reversed", va="center", ha="left", fontsize=6.9,
            color=style.INK)
ax.set_yticks(ys, [LABELS[k] for k in tab.index], fontsize=7.2)
ax.set_xlim(0, tab["n"].max() * 1.32)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7)
ax.set_xlabel("Reviews, 2021–2025", fontsize=7.6)
ax.legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=7.2)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Two patterns are worth carrying into a game. First, catch-or-no-catch rulings make up about
`{python} S["catch_share"]` of all the recorded reviews, which is why the next section spends so long on the
catch. Second, rulings of a *catch* are reviewed more than twice as often as rulings of *incomplete*
(and overturned at a similar rate: `{python} S["catch_rev"]` against `{python} S["incomp_rev"]`). Part of
that is the booth looking at every touchdown catch. Part of it is by design: officials are taught to rule
the play that keeps the ball alive when in doubt, for a reason the 2008 story below makes plain.

## The catch

Nothing in the rulebook has caused more arguments than the definition of a catch, and the reason is the
stakes. Whether a pass was caught decides more than one play. If it was a catch and the ball then comes
loose, it's a **fumble**: a live ball anyone can recover. If it wasn't, it's an **incomplete pass**: the ball
is dead and the offense keeps it. A single definition separates "the offense keeps the ball and loses a
down" from "the defense may have it". So the rule has to draw a line between *possessing* a ball and merely
*touching* it, at full speed, in the air, often while someone is hitting the receiver.

Today's rule, rewritten in 2018, says a player has made a
[**catch**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-catch-completed-pass) when, in bounds, he does three things in
order:[^catchrule]

1. **Control.** He secures control of the ball in his hands or arms before it touches the ground.
2. **Feet (or a body part) down.** He touches the ground in bounds with both feet, or with any part of his
   body other than his hands (a knee, a hip, an elbow).
3. **Time.** After the first two, he makes an *act common to the game*: tucks the ball away, turns upfield,
   takes an extra step, reaches the ball toward the line, wards off a defender. Or he keeps control long
   enough that he *could* have.

Three clarifications do most of the work on replays.

- **Slight movement isn't a loss of control.** A ball that shifts in his hands while he keeps his hands on
  it is still controlled. Bobbling it and then securing it is fine too, as long as it never touches the
  ground in between.
- **The ground matters only before gate 3.** If he finishes gate 3 on his feet (a third step, a turn, a
  reach) and *then* falls and the ball comes out, it was a catch and then a fumble, or simply a catch if he
  was down by contact. But if he is falling *while* he catches it, so that he hits the ground before he has
  had time for any football act, the ground is part of the catch: he must keep control when he lands. If
  the ball pops loose and touches the ground then, the pass is incomplete.
- **A tie goes to the offense.** If an offensive and a defensive player catch the ball at the same moment and
  both keep it, it's the offense's ball. If one had it first and the other wrestled in, it belongs to the
  first.

An interception is judged by exactly the same three gates.

```{python}
#| label: fig-catch
#| fig-cap: "The catch rule as a replay official applies it (NFL rule since 2018). A pass must pass all three gates in order. Failing gate 1 or 2 means incomplete. At gate 3, a receiver who hasn't yet had time for a football act when he hits the ground (or lands out of bounds) must keep control through it, or the pass is incomplete. Once gate 3 is passed, losing the ball means a catch and then a fumble. The same test decides an interception."
fig, ax = canvas(6.5, 5.9)
G, YES, NO = "#efeee9", "#d4efe5", "#fbe3e1"
cx, rx = 32, 80
fbox(ax, cx, 86, 46, 6.0, "The pass arrives", fc=G, tfs=8.2)
gates = [
    (71, "1. Control", "secured in his hands or arms before\nthe ball touches the ground? (slight\nmovement or a bobble he secures is fine)"),
    (51, "2. Feet down in bounds", "both feet, or any body part\nother than his hands?"),
    (31, "3. Time", "an act common to the game (tuck, turn\nupfield, extra step, reach, ward off),\nor control long enough to make one?"),
]
farrow(ax, (cx, 82.9), (cx, 78.4))
for i, (y, t, b) in enumerate(gates):
    fbox(ax, cx, y, 46, 13.4, t, b, fc=G, tfs=7.8, bfs=6.5)
    nxt = gates[i + 1][0] + 6.8 if i < 2 else 15.6
    farrow(ax, (cx, y - 6.8), (cx, nxt), "yes", toff=(3.4, 0))
fbox(ax, rx, 71, 30, 10.5, "INCOMPLETE", "he never secured it before\nit hit the ground", fc=NO, ec=RED)
fbox(ax, rx, 51, 30, 10.5, "INCOMPLETE", "out of bounds (in the\nend zone: no touchdown)", fc=NO, ec=RED)
fbox(ax, rx, 31, 30, 12.0, "HIT THE GROUND FIRST", "falling as he caught it, or\nlanding out of bounds: did he\nkeep control through it?", fc="#fdf3d8",
     ec=style.LINE_TO_GAIN, tfs=7.2)
fbox(ax, rx, 11, 30, 8.0, "INCOMPLETE", "the ball came loose", fc=NO, ec=RED)
for y in (71, 51):
    farrow(ax, (cx + 23.2, y), (rx - 15.2, y), "no", toff=(0, 1.9))
farrow(ax, (cx + 23.2, 31), (rx - 15.2, 31), "not yet", toff=(0, 1.9))
farrow(ax, (rx, 24.9), (rx, 15.1), "no", toff=(3.0, 0))
fbox(ax, cx, 9.5, 46, 12.0, "CATCH", "if the ball comes loose now: a fumble\n(live ball). If he's in the end zone,\nor reaches it over the line: touchdown", fc=YES,
     ec=GREEN, tfs=8.6)
farrow(ax, (rx - 15.2, 27.5), (cx + 23.4, 13.5), "yes, kept it", toff=(2.0, 2.2))
plt.show()
```

### Why the rule was rewritten

For most of the 2010s the rule had an extra clause that produced some of the most hated rulings in league
history. A receiver who went to the ground "in the process of the catch" had to keep control of the ball
*after* hitting the ground, the so-called *survive the ground* requirement, no matter how many steps he had
taken or how obviously he had possessed it. The clause was meant to make the rule objective: instead of
asking officials to judge whether a player had possession long enough, it gave them a test they could see on
video. The trouble was that the objective test kept ruling against what everyone watching had seen. Three
plays made it untenable:[^catchhist]

- **Calvin Johnson, Lions at Bears, September 12, 2010.** Trailing 19–14 with 31 seconds left, Johnson
  caught a pass in the end zone, landed with both feet and his backside, and put the ball down on the turf
  as he rolled to get up. Ruled incomplete; the booth upheld it. The Lions lost by five, and "the Calvin
  Johnson rule" entered the vocabulary.
- **Dez Bryant, Cowboys at Packers, divisional playoffs, January 11, 2015.** On fourth-and-2 late in the
  game, Bryant caught a deep ball, took three steps as he fell, reached for the goal line, and the ball
  moved when it hit the turf at the 1. Ruled a catch, reversed on Green Bay's challenge; the Packers won
  (the Film room below walks through it).
- **Jesse James, Patriots at Steelers, December 17, 2017.** With 34 seconds left and Pittsburgh down
  27–24, James caught a short pass a few yards from the goal line, went to a knee *untouched* (so he wasn't down: in the NFL
  a runner needs contact, as the next section explains), and lunged across the goal line; the ball moved
  as it hit the turf. Ruled a touchdown, reversed by the booth. The Steelers lost the game and, as it
  turned out, home-field advantage in the playoffs.

The league's competition committee rewrote the rule that offseason, and the owners approved it 32–0 in
March 2018. Here is precisely what changed. Under the old rule, a receiver who went to the ground "in the
process of the catch" had to survive the ground *however many steps or reaches he had made on the way
down*: falling cancelled them. Under the new rule, a football act made before the ball comes loose (a third
step, reaching the ball toward the line, or simply time enough to make one) finishes the catch, even if he
is falling at the time, and only a receiver who hits the ground *before* he has made one still has to
survive it. The 2018 announcement called that act a "football move"; the rulebook calls it an "act common
to the game". The league's football chiefs said publicly that under it, Bryant's and James's catches would
have counted: their three steps and their reaches were football acts, made before the ball touched
down.[^catchnew]

Would Calvin Johnson's? Try it with the gates. Control: yes, high in the end zone. Feet: both feet, then
his backside. Time: the argument. He went to the ground as he caught it, so he must keep control through
the landing unless he had time for a football act first. If you see him land, hold the ball, and only then
use it to push himself up, he had the time, and it's a touchdown today. If you see one continuous fall
with the ball coming loose as part of it, it's still incomplete. The league never ruled on it publicly,
and that is the honest answer: the new rule turned a mechanical question into a judgment about time.

The trade-off is worth naming, because it's the same trade the whole replay system keeps making. The old
rule was objective and produced absurd results; the new rule matches what people see, at the price of a
judgment call ("did he have time?") at the center of it. Disputes didn't disappear; they moved from "did
the ball move when he hit the ground?" to "was that lunge a football act or part of the fall?"

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"The ball touched the ground, so it's incomplete." The ball is allowed to touch the ground during a catch,
as long as the receiver keeps control of it, with his hands under it or the ball pinned to his body. What it
can't do is help him: a ball trapped against the turf with no hand under it, or one that pops loose when he
lands before he has had time for a football act, is incomplete.
:::

### Sidelines and end zones

Two places put extra weight on gate 2. At the **sideline**, a receiver needs both feet (or another body
part) down in bounds with control; one foot, as in college football, isn't enough. Since 2008 there has been
no "force-out" ruling either: a receiver pushed out of bounds in the air before getting both feet down has
not caught the ball, however sure the official is that he would have landed in bounds. (The one exception
is a receiver who has control and is held up and *carried* out by a defender: that is still a catch.)[^forceout] And
because a toe-tap catch leaves no time for a football act before he goes out of bounds, he must keep control
as he falls out; a ball jarred loose when he hits the ground out of bounds is incomplete.

In the **end zone**, the catch is the touchdown, so the receiver must complete all three steps there. That
is different from a runner who already has the ball: for him, the ball only has to touch the plane of the
goal line (the [end zone](../01-foundations/01-01-the-game-in-fifteen-minutes.qmd) is generous that way).
Under the 2018 rule, a receiver who completes the catch short of the goal line and then reaches the ball
across it has scored, which is how Jesse James's play would be ruled today.

## Down, progress and the whistle

A play ends when the ball becomes dead, and most of the time that means a ball carrier going down. The NFL's
definition is different from the one you may know from college. A runner is
[**down by contact**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-down-by-contact) when any part of his body other than
his hands or feet touches the ground *and he has been touched by an opponent*. The order of those two can
go either way. If nobody touched him, he isn't down: a running back who slips on wet turf, or a returner who
kneels to field a bouncing kick, may get up and keep running. But if a defender touches him *while* he is
on the ground, he is down right there, which is why defenders are coached to "touch him down" rather than
assume the play is over. In college football the runner is down as soon as his knee touches, contact or
not.[^downrule] (A runner who slides feet-first or simply gives himself up is down where he does it; that's
how quarterbacks protect themselves.)

The order of events matters more than anything else on these plays. If the ball comes out *before* the knee
(or elbow, or hip) touches after contact, it's a fumble: live, and anyone's. If the knee touches first, the
runner was down and the ball coming out afterward doesn't matter. On television these are separated by a
few frames of video, which is why they're among the most-reviewed rulings in the data above.

```{python}
#| label: fig-down-fumble
#| fig-cap: "Down or fumble? It depends on the order of three events: the defender's contact, the ball coming loose, and the runner's knee (or any body part other than a hand or foot) touching the ground. Top: the ball comes out first, so it's a fumble and the ball is live. Middle: the knee touches first, after contact, so he's down and the play is dead before the ball comes loose. Bottom: nobody touched him, so in the NFL he isn't down; he can get up and keep running, unless a defender touches him while he's on the ground (in college he'd be down at once). Either way, the ball is spotted where it was when he went down, not where his knee was."
fig, ax = canvas(6.5, 2.5, xmax=100, ymax=39)
rows = [
    (31.0, [(10, "contact"), (31, "ball comes out"), (52, "knee down")], "FUMBLE", "live ball: anyone may recover", RED),
    (19.5, [(10, "contact"), (31, "knee down"), (52, "ball comes out")], "DOWN", "dead: ball spotted where it was\nwhen the knee touched", GREEN),
    (8.0, [(10, "slips, untouched"), (31, "knee down"), (52, "gets up, runs on")], "NOT DOWN", "unless touched while on the\nground (college: down)", style.OFFENSE_DARK),
]
ax.text(3, 37.0, "time →", fontsize=7.0, color=style.INK_2, ha="left", va="center")
for y, evs, verdict, sub, col in rows:
    ax.plot([3, 62], [y, y], color=style.BASELINE, lw=1.2, zorder=1)
    for i, (x, lab) in enumerate(evs):
        ax.plot(x, y, marker="o", ms=7, color=col if i == 1 else style.INK_2, zorder=3)
        ax.text(x, y + 2.6, lab, fontsize=6.9, ha="center", va="center", color=style.INK, zorder=4)
    ax.text(66, y + 1.3, verdict, fontsize=8.2, fontweight="bold", color=col, ha="left", va="center")
    ax.text(66, y - 1.4, sub, fontsize=6.5, color=style.INK_2, ha="left", va="top", linespacing=1.1)
plt.show()
```

**Forward progress** decides *where* the play ended. You met it in
[Downs, Distance, and Field Position](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd): the
ball is spotted at the farthest point it reached toward the goal line before the runner was stopped, not
where he ended up after a pile drove him back. The same idea tells officials when to blow the whistle. A
runner wrapped up and held upright, his legs still churning, has had his forward progress stopped even
though he hasn't gone down, and the officials will whistle the play dead rather than let a pile of
defenders keep shoving him backward (or strip the ball from a man who has stopped moving forward). It also
protects runners at the goal line: a back who gets the ball across the plane and is then knocked back
into the field has scored. The protection covers only being *driven* back, though: a quarterback who
retreats on his own and is sacked is spotted where he goes down, which is why a sack costs yards. And it
affects the clock: a runner stopped in bounds and then shoved out of bounds was down *in bounds*, so the
clock keeps running, a detail that matters in [the two-minute drill](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd).

### The whistle, and the 2008 lesson

The whistle is the one tool officials can't take back. Once it blows, the play is dead, whatever happens
next. (When an official blows one by mistake with the ball still live, the rules try to undo the damage:
the team with the ball can usually take it where the whistle killed the play or replay the down, and a
pass in the air at the whistle is simply replayed.)[^whistle] That used to put replay in an impossible position: if an official ruled a play over (an incomplete
pass, a runner down) and the video showed a fumble, replay could fix the ruling but could not know who would
have recovered the ball if everyone had kept playing.

The play that made everyone face this came on September 14, 2008. Denver trailed San Diego 38–31 with 1:17
left, second-and-goal at the 1. Jay Cutler dropped back, and the ball slipped out of his hand as he started
to throw; a Charger fell on it. Referee Ed Hochuli ruled it an incomplete pass and blew his whistle. Replay
showed a fumble, but because the whistle had already killed the play, the Chargers couldn't be given the
ball. Denver kept it at the 10, where Cutler had lost it, scored on fourth-and-goal with 29 seconds left,
went for two, and won 39–38.[^hochuli]
Hochuli, one of the most respected referees of his era, publicly apologized.

Two things changed. In 2009 the owners passed what was quickly nicknamed the "Hochuli rule": replay may now
award the ball to the team that recovered it when the recovery is clear and in the *immediate continuing
action*, even after a whistle.[^hochulirule] And the officials' habit changed:
on a bang-bang fumble, they are taught to hold the whistle, let the players finish the scramble for the
ball, and rule a fumble when in doubt, because replay can turn a fumble back into a dead ball cleanly but
can't recreate a recovery that never happened. That is why you now see plays continue for a few seconds after
a runner seems to be down, and a defender scooping up a loose ball and running the other way while
everyone else has stopped.

## Pass or fumble: the quarterback's arm

A close cousin of down-or-fumble is pass-or-fumble, and it comes up every time a pass rusher hits a
quarterback as he throws. The rule is about the arm. Once the quarterback, holding the ball, starts his arm
moving forward to throw, anything that comes out is a forward pass, and if it hits the ground it's
incomplete. If he loses the ball *before* his arm starts forward, or while he is pulling it back down
to tuck it after deciding not to throw, it's a fumble.

The second half of that sentence was not always true. Until 2013 the rulebook had the **tuck rule**: if the
quarterback started forward and then brought the ball back toward his body, it was still a pass until he
had tucked it all the way in. It is remembered for one snowy night in Foxborough: the divisional playoff in
January 2002, when Tom Brady lost the ball under a hit from Charles Woodson late in the fourth quarter, the
Raiders recovered, and replay applied the tuck rule to call it an incomplete pass. New England kept the
ball, tied the game with a field goal and won in overtime, the first playoff run of a dynasty. The league
abolished the rule in 2013.[^tuck] Today the same play is a fumble.

Who reviews it depends on the call on the field. When the field rules a fumble that the defense recovered,
it's a turnover, so the booth reviews it automatically. When the field rules an incomplete pass, there's no
turnover to trigger the booth, so before the two-minute warning the defense's coach usually has to throw his
red flag (unless replay assist steps in on the possession), which is the moment you see a coach grab it
on a strip-sack ruled incomplete. Either way, watch
the arm, not the ball: if the arm was coming forward with the ball in the hand, it's a pass.

## A fumble through the end zone

Now the harshest rule in the book. When a fumble goes out of bounds, the general rule is generous to the
team that fumbled: it keeps the ball. If the ball went out going backward, it's spotted where it went out;
if it went out going *forward*, it comes back to the spot of the fumble, so that nobody gains yards by
fumbling forward on purpose.

The exception is the opponent's end zone. A
[**fumble through the end zone**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-fumble-through-the-end-zone-touchback),
a ball fumbled forward into the end zone that goes out of bounds there, out the side or out the back, is a
**touchback**: the defense gets the ball at its own 20, even though no defender ever touched it.[^fumbleoob]
A fumble that stays *in* the end zone is simpler: if the offense falls on it there, it's a touchdown (on fourth
down or late in a half, only the man who fumbled may, as the box below explains); if the defense does, it's a touchback. And the mirror image works against the offense in its own end zone: a
ball it fumbles there that goes out of bounds (or one it fumbles in the field that it sends back into its
own end zone and out) is a **safety**, because the offense supplied the push that put the ball there.

```{python}
#| label: fig-fumble-oob
#| fig-cap: "Three fumbles out of bounds near the goal line, offense moving up the page. Left: the ball squirts forward and out at the 2: the offense keeps it, but back at the 4, the spot of the fumble, because a forward fumble can't gain ground. Middle: knocked loose at the 1, it bounces into the end zone and out the side: a touchback, and the defense takes over at its own 20. Right: the ball goes backward and out at the 8: the offense keeps it where it went out. The X marks the fumble (D is the defender who knocked it loose), the dashed brown line the ball's path."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(6.5, 3.9))
cases = [
    ((-2.0, 18.0), (2.0, 19.2), [(2.0, 19.2), (3.2, 21.4), (4.0, 23.58), (4.3, 24.8)], "offense's ball\nat the 4", (2.0, 12.2), style.OFFENSE_DARK),
    ((-1.5, 18.5), (5.0, 21.0), [(5.0, 21.0), (7.8, 22.4), (11.5, 23.58), (12.2, 24.8)], "touchback:\ndefense's ball\nat its 20", (11.6, 14.2), RED),
    ((-1.0, 16.5), (2.0, 19.5), [(2.0, 19.5), (0.5, 21.6), (-2.0, 23.58), (-2.6, 24.8)], "offense's ball\nat the 8", (-4.6, 15.5), style.OFFENSE_DARK),
]
for ax, (start, fum, ballpath, verdict, vat, col) in zip(axes, cases):
    rb = O("RB", "RB", start[0], start[1], "R")
    q = Play([rb], [D("DB", "DB", fum[0] + 1.0, fum[1] - 2.3, "D")], los=104, ball_y="right", to_go=None)
    q.run("RB", [fum], absolute=True)
    fld = q.draw(ax=ax, lateral=(7.0, 29.5), window=(-6.5, 16.5), title=False)
    no_numbers(ax)
    say(fld, q, 2.0, 26.6, "out of bounds", fs=5.6, box=False, rot=90)
    for dd, lab in ((1.0, "5"), (-4.0, "10")):
        say(fld, q, dd + 0.6, 9.0, lab, fs=5.8, color=style.MUTED, box=False)
    xmark(fld, q, *fum)
    path_arrow(fld, q, ballpath)
    say(fld, q, vat[0], vat[1], verdict, color=col, fs=6.6, weight="bold")
    say(fld, q, 6.0, 12.0, "goal line", fs=5.8, color=style.INK_2)
    say(fld, q, 14.4, 11.0, "end line", fs=5.8, color=style.INK_2)
    say(fld, q, -0.9, 11.8, "line of scrimmage", fs=5.0, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
for ax, lab in zip(axes, ["Forward, out at the 2", "Into the end zone, out", "Backward, out at the 8"]):
    ax.set_title(lab, fontsize=7.8, color=style.INK, loc="left", fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.4)
plt.show()
```

Why would the rules punish the offense so hard? The logic is about territory, not possession. The end zone
belongs to the defending team. When a ball goes dead in or behind your end zone because of something the
other team did (a punt rolls through, a kickoff sails out the back), the result is a touchback, your ball
at your 20, like the [touchbacks on punts](09-01-kicking-and-punting.qmd). A fumble into your end zone and
out is treated the same way: the offense put the ball there, it died there, and it's yours. The rule is
consistent; it just doesn't feel fair, because the offense had the ball a moment earlier and the defense
did nothing to earn it. It is one of the most criticized rules in the book, and ideas to soften it
(giving the ball back to the offense at the spot of the fumble, say) come up every few years. The league's
competition committee looked at it and kept it in 2017 and again in February 2024, after a playoff fumble
through the end zone, arguing that the ball carrier is responsible for the ball and noting that nobody had
come up with a workable alternative. It is unchanged in the 2026 rulebook.[^fumblecomm]

The rule shapes technique. It's why coaches drill runners and receivers to carry the ball in the arm away
from the defenders near the goal line, why a ball carrier stretching for the pylon is taking a real gamble,
and why defenders near the goal line punch at the ball instead of wrapping up. A clean tackle at the 1 gives
the offense first-and-goal; a punched ball through the end zone gives the defense the ball at the 20.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists: the fourth-down fumble rule"}
One more fumble rule has a famous origin. On September 10, 1978, with the Raiders trailing the Chargers in
the final seconds, Ken Stabler, about to be sacked, fumbled the ball forward; teammates batted and kicked it
toward the goal line, and Dave Casper fell on it in the end zone for the winning touchdown. The "Holy
Roller" was legal then. The next season the league made it impossible: on fourth down, and on any down after
the two-minute warning, only the player who fumbled may recover and advance the ball. If a teammate
recovers it, the ball comes back to the spot of the fumble (or the spot of recovery, if that is behind
it).[^holyroller] The rule exists to stop an offense from fumbling forward on purpose when it has nothing
left to lose.
:::

## Backward passes and forward passes

Football allows exactly **one forward pass per play**, and it must be thrown from behind the line of
scrimmage. It allows any number of [**backward passes**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-backward-pass)
(also called [**laterals**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-lateral)), from anywhere, by anyone, at any
time. The two are treated very differently when they hit the ground:

- A **forward pass** that hits the ground is **incomplete**. The ball is dead, and the offense keeps it.
- A **backward pass** that hits the ground is **still live**, exactly like a fumble. Either team may recover
  it, and either team may advance it.

Which is which? The test is the ball's direction: compare the yard line where it left the passer's hand
with the yard line where it is first touched (or first hits the ground). If the second is closer to the
opponent's goal, the pass was forward. If it's the same yard line or behind, the pass was backward, so a
pass thrown perfectly parallel to the line counts as **backward**.[^lateral] Notice that it's the ball's
path that counts, not the players' positions on the field. (This chapter calls the yard line where the ball
leaves the passer's hand the *release line*; that's our label for the diagrams, not a rulebook term.)

The forward pass's two limits are fouls of their own, and the line judge watches for the first. A forward
pass is **illegal** if the passer's *entire body* and the ball are beyond the line of scrimmage when he lets
go, which is the call you see on a quarterback who scrambles up to the line and flips it at the last
moment: one foot still behind the line keeps it legal. A **second forward pass** on the same play is illegal
too. Either costs a loss of down and 5 yards.

```{python}
#| label: fig-lateral
#| fig-cap: "Forward or backward is decided by the yard line where the ball leaves the passer's hand (dashed 'release line') and the yard line where it's first touched. From the shotgun, the quarterback catches the snap five yards deep. A pitch to the running back (1), who has swung out to the right and slightly back, is caught behind the release line: a backward pass, live if it hits the ground. A bubble screen (2) to the slot receiver, who has bowed back from his alignment to the release line, is parallel, which counts as backward. A quick screen to the outside receiver (3) is caught about five yards ahead of the release line: a forward pass, incomplete (and dead) if it's dropped."
off = offense("gun_2x2")
off = [q.moved(w=2.6) if q.key == "RB" else q for q in off]
lp = Play(off, None, los=40, to_go=None)
lp.path("RB", [(-6.0, 4.6), (-6.4, 7.8)], absolute=True)           # swings out to take the pitch
lp.path("H", [(-3.2, -10.2), (-5.1, -10.9), (-5.4, -10.6)], absolute=True)   # the bubble: bows back
fld = lp.draw(lateral=(-19.5, 19.5), window=(-12.0, 4.5), title=False)
ax = fld.ax
no_numbers(ax)
rel = (-5.4, 0.3)
x0, y0 = XY(fld, lp, rel[0], -18.0)
x1, y1 = XY(fld, lp, rel[0], 18.0)
ax.plot([x0, x1], [y0, y1], color=PURPLE, lw=1.2, ls=(0, (4, 3)), zorder=2)
say(fld, lp, -4.4, -15.6, "release line", color=PURPLE, fs=6.6, weight="bold")
for tgt, col, lab, lat in [((-6.6, 7.4), GREEN, "1  backward:\nlive if dropped", (-9.6, 7.6)),
                           ((-5.4, -10.6), GREEN, "2  parallel = backward:\nlive if dropped", (-8.8, -10.0)),
                           ((-0.9, 14.0), RED, "3  forward:\nincomplete if dropped", (1.9, 9.4))]:
    path_arrow(fld, lp, [rel, tgt], color=style.BALL, lw=1.5)
    say(fld, lp, lat[0], lat[1], lab, color=col, fs=6.6, weight="bold")
say(fld, lp, 1.0, -3.0, "line of scrimmage", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fs=6.2)
plt.show()
```

Why does a dropped backward pass stay live? Because the rules treat it as the normal case. A backward pass
is just a handoff through the air: the ball stays a runner's ball, and if he doesn't catch it, it's loose,
like any fumble. The *forward* pass is the special case, the one the rules ration (one per play, from
behind the line) and give a special ending: when it fails, the play stops and the offense keeps the ball,
paying with the down. The result shows up in three places on a broadcast:

- **Pitches and option plays.** A pitch on the
  [option](../03-the-run-game/03-04-option-football.qmd) is a backward pass. Drop it and you've fumbled, in
  effect, which is why option teams drill the pitch relentlessly.
- **Screens.** Most screens thrown from the shotgun are forward passes, because the quarterback releases
  the ball five or six yards behind the line and the receiver catches it closer to the line than that. But
  a bubble or swing screen to a player who has drifted back level with the quarterback may be backward, and
  a defender who sees it hit the ground should pick it up and run. Coaches teach defenders to scoop up every
  loose screen and let the officials sort it out. The rules on linemen downfield follow the same line: the
  [illegal-man-downfield rule](../04-the-passing-game/04-06-rpos.qmd) applies only when a forward pass is
  thrown beyond the line, so on a true backward pass linemen may already be blocking downfield.
- **Last-play desperation.** The multi-lateral kickoff return or final snap, the ball pitched backward
  again and again, is legal because every pitch is backward.

The most famous backward pass in NFL history came in a wild-card game on January 8, 2000. Buffalo had just
kicked a go-ahead field goal with 16 seconds left. On the kickoff, Tennessee's Lorenzo Neal handed the ball
to tight end Frank Wycheck, who turned and threw it across the field to Kevin Dyson, who ran 75 yards
untouched down the sideline for the winning touchdown. Replay looked at whether Wycheck's throw had gone
forward. It hadn't been shown to: the ruling of a legal lateral stood, and the "Music City Miracle" became
the standard illustration of the rule that what counts is the ball's path from hand to hands.[^musiccity]

## Intentional grounding and the tackle box

[Quarterback Play](../04-the-passing-game/04-07-quarterback-play.qmd) introduced the
[throwaway](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-throwaway) and the rule that limits it. Here is the full rule,
and the reasoning behind it.

[**Intentional grounding**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-intentional-grounding) is a foul when a passer
who is facing an imminent loss of yardage because of the rush throws a pass that isn't in the direction and
vicinity of an eligible receiver. (The rulebook says *originally* eligible: eligible when the ball was
snapped, so a lineman who has wandered downfield doesn't count as a target.) Three conditions, all
needed:[^grounding]

1. **Pressure.** He must be facing a likely sack. A quarterback under no pressure who throws the ball into
   the turf has wasted a down, but he hasn't grounded it.
2. **No realistic target.** The pass isn't thrown near an eligible receiver. "Near" is a judgment, and
   throwing the ball well over the head of a covered receiver in the right part of the field counts.
3. **Inside the tackle box.** The [**tackle box**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tackle-box), which the
   rulebook calls the *pocket area*, is the region between the outside edges of where the two offensive
   tackles lined up, running from the line of scrimmage all the way back to the offense's own end line.
   It's fixed by where the *tackles* aligned at the snap: a tight end lined up outside a tackle doesn't
   widen it, and it doesn't move when the quarterback does.

The exception is what makes the box matter: **a passer who is or has been outside the tackle box may throw
the ball away freely, as long as it lands at or beyond the line of scrimmage** (extended to the sidelines),
including out of bounds past it. Since the 2024 rulebook he counts as outside the box if any part of his
body, or the ball, is outside it. And "has been" means what it says: a quarterback who escapes the box and
then drifts back inside it keeps the exception for the rest of the play.

The penalty is built to cost about what the sack would have: **loss of down and 10 yards** from the previous
spot, or loss of down at the spot of the pass if that is farther back, and **a safety** if he throws it
from his own end zone. The other exception you'll see every week is the **spike**: a quarterback who throws
the ball straight into the ground immediately after taking the snap, to stop the clock, isn't penalized;
it costs a down and nothing else. Spikes belong to the end-of-half clock game, which is in
[The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd).

```{python}
#| label: fig-tackle-box
#| fig-cap: "Intentional grounding backed up at the offense's own 4, where the tackle box (shaded) runs back into the end zone. Quarterback A, inside the box and in his end zone, throws to an empty part of the field (1): grounding, and from the end zone that's a safety. Throwing it over the covered tight end's head instead (2) is a legal throwaway. Quarterback B has escaped the box with a defender closing: throwing it out of bounds past the line of scrimmage (3) is legal even though no one is near, but a throw that lands out of bounds short of the line (4) is grounding, also a safety from the end zone. Notice that throw 1 lands past the line too: inside the box, reaching the line doesn't help."
off = offense("gun_2x2")
off = [q for q in off if q.key in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT", "Y")]
off = [q.moved(d=7.5, w=8.0) if q.key == "Y" else q for q in off]
gp = Play(off + [O("QB", "QB", -6.0, 0.0, "A")],
          [D("LB", "MIKE", 9.0, 9.2, "M"), D("E1", "DE", -4.8, -2.2, "E"), D("E2", "DE", -5.2, 2.0, "T"),
           D("E3", "DE", -6.4, 9.4, "E")],                     # closing on quarterback B
          los=14, ball_y="right", to_go=None)
fld = gp.draw(lateral=(-20.5, 27.2), window=(-14.5, 15.5), title=False)
ax = fld.ax
no_numbers(ax)
tackle_box(ax, fld, gp, -14.0)
qbB = (-7.5, 12.5)
draw_marker(ax, *XY(fld, gp, *qbB), "off", "B", fld.pts_per_yard())
path_arrow(fld, gp, [(-6.0, 0.0), (-1.0, -3.5), (6.0, -6.0)], color=RED, lw=1.6)
path_arrow(fld, gp, [(-6.0, 0.0), (5.0, 6.0), (11.0, 9.0)], color=GREEN, lw=1.6)
path_arrow(fld, gp, [qbB, (2.5, 24.4)], color=GREEN, lw=1.6)
path_arrow(fld, gp, [qbB, (-3.2, 24.4)], color=RED, lw=1.6)
say(fld, gp, 8.8, -8.5, "1  grounding: inside the box,\nthe line doesn't help (safety)", color=RED, fs=6.8, weight="bold")
say(fld, gp, 12.8, 5.0, "2  legal: near Y", color=GREEN, fs=6.8, weight="bold")
say(fld, gp, 5.4, 15.8, "3  legal: out of\nbounds past the line", color=GREEN, fs=6.8, weight="bold")
say(fld, gp, -11.0, 16.6, "4  grounding: short\nof the line (safety)", color=RED, fs=6.8, weight="bold")
say(fld, gp, -11.7, 0.0, "tackle box\n(back to the end line)", color=PURPLE, fs=6.4, weight="bold")
say(fld, gp, -3.0, -10.5, "goal line", fs=6.0)
say(fld, gp, 1.2, -16.0, "line of scrimmage", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fs=6.2)
say(fld, gp, -9.0, -12.0, "end zone", fs=6.4, color=style.INK_2)
xs_, ys_ = XY(fld, gp, 6.0, 25.3)
ax.text(xs_, ys_, "out of bounds", rotation=90, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.0, color=style.INK_2)
plt.show()
```

Why draw the line at the box? The rule is balancing two things. A sack is something the defense earned:
it beat the blockers. If a quarterback could always throw the ball into the ground to avoid one, the pass
rush would lose much of its value, so inside the pocket, where the defense has him trapped, he must at least
throw toward someone. But a quarterback who has escaped the pocket has beaten the rush himself, and he's
usually near the sideline with defenders closing; letting him throw it away (provided it reaches the line,
so he can't just dump it at his feet) rewards the escape and spares him a hit. The 2024 wording, counting
the ball or any body part outside the box, tilted that balance a little further toward the quarterback.

The best-known grounding call of recent decades shows the safety clause at work: on New England's first
offensive play of Super Bowl XLVI, February 5, 2012, Tom Brady, pressured in his own end zone, threw deep down
the middle to nobody. Grounding from the end zone is a safety, and the Giants led 2–0 before the Patriots had
gained a yard. They won by four.[^xlvi]

The "has been outside" clause is the subtle part, and it's easiest to see in motion.

```{python}
#| label: fig-grounding-anim
#| fig-cap: "Once outside, always outside (simulated tracking in Big Data Bowl format; an illustrative play). 0.4 s: the quarterback finishes his drop in the middle of the tackle box (shaded), so a throwaway must go near a receiver. 2.1 s: pressure flushes him to his right, well outside the box; the grounding exception is now on. 3.4 s: he steps back up inside the box, but he has been outside, so the exception stays on for the rest of the play. 4.4 s: he has thrown it away (dashed brown line) into open grass on the left, away from every receiver, and it landed past the line of scrimmage: legal, no flag. Had it landed short of the line, it would be grounding."
off = offense("gun_2x2")
dfn = defense("nickel", "two_high", off)
dfn = [q.moved(d=6.0, w=-3.5) if q.key == "WILL" else q for q in dfn]
sp = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10)
for k in ("X", "Z"):
    sp.route(k, r.go(12))
for k in ("H", "Y"):
    sp.route(k, r.seam(11))
for dk, rk in (("LCB", "X"), ("RCB", "Z"), ("NB", "H"), ("SS", "Y")):
    sp.man(dk, rk)
for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):                  # the line sets and holds
    sp.block(k, pts=[(-1.3, 0.0)])
sp.block("RB", pts=[(0.6, -2.2)])                        # the back stays in to block
# the quarterback: drops, is flushed well right (out of the box), then steps back up inside it
sp.path("QB", [(-2.0, 0.0), (-2.8, 8.5), (-1.0, 1.5)], speed=5.0)
sp.path("SDT", [(-0.4, 0.9)], absolute=True); sp.path("WDT", [(-0.4, -0.9)], absolute=True)
sp.path("WDE", [(-3.5, -4.5), (-7.0, -1.2), (-8.8, 0.6)], absolute=True, speed=5.5)   # flushes him, overruns
sp.path("SDE", [(-1.8, 4.6)], absolute=True)                                            # held up by the tackle...
sp.path("SDE", [(-6.0, 10.8)], absolute=True, delay=1.0)                                # ...then closes outside
sp.drop("MIKE", (6.0, 2.5)); sp.drop("FS", (13.0, -7.0))
trk = sp.to_tracking(t_after=2.4)
trk = trk[trk.time <= 4.6].copy()
T_THROW, LAND = 3.5, (2.5, -5.5)                         # lands past the line, in open grass
qb_at = sp.position("QB", T_THROW)
ball = trk.side == "ball"
pre = ball & (trk.time > 0.15) & (trk.time < T_THROW)       # carried in his right hand, not over his face
trk.loc[pre, "y"] -= 0.8
m = ball & (trk.time >= T_THROW)
tt = trk.loc[m, "time"].to_numpy()
T_FLIGHT = np.hypot(*(np.array(LAND) - qb_at)) / 16.0
f = np.clip((tt - T_THROW) / T_FLIGHT, 0, 1)
bd = qb_at[0] + f * (LAND[0] - qb_at[0])
bw = qb_at[1] + f * (LAND[1] - qb_at[1])
trk.loc[m, "x"], trk.loc[m, "y"] = sp.to_abs(bd, bw)
GNOTES = [("inside the box:\nthrow near a receiver", PURPLE), ("well outside:\nexception on", GREEN),
          ("back inside, but has\nbeen outside: still on", GREEN), ("lands past the line:\nlegal throwaway", GREEN)]


def g_decor(fld, t):
    tackle_box(fld.ax, fld, sp, -13.0, alpha=0.12)
    if t >= T_THROW:                                    # the ball's flight so far
        g = min(1.0, (t - T_THROW) / T_FLIGHT)
        end = (qb_at[0] + g * (LAND[0] - qb_at[0]), qb_at[1] + g * (LAND[1] - qb_at[1]))
        if g > 0.05:
            path_arrow(fld, sp, [tuple(qb_at), end], color=style.BALL, lw=1.6, head=10)


def g_notes(fld, i, t):
    txt, col = GNOTES[i]
    say(fld, sp, -10.8, -12.0, txt, color=col, fs=6.6 if PDF else 8.0, weight="bold")


show_scene(sp, trk, [0.4, 2.1, 3.4, 4.4], window=(-13.5, 15.5), lateral=(-19.5, 19.5), decor=g_decor,
           notes=g_notes)
```

## The measurement: chains, cameras, and the spot

[Downs, Distance, and Field Position](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd)
described the chain crew and its century-old ritual: two sticks joined by ten yards of chain, carried onto
the field and stretched out to see whether the ball's nose had reached the front stick. Since 2025 that walk
is mostly gone. A [**virtual measurement**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-virtual-measurement), often
called a [**Hawk-Eye measurement**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hawk-eye-measurement) after the Sony
system that does it, uses six 8K cameras around the stadium to measure the distance from where the ball sits
to the line to gain, and hands the answer to the officials in about 30 seconds, while a virtual graphic of
the measurement plays on the broadcast and the stadium screens. The chain crew stays on the sideline as the
visible marker for players and coaches, and as a backup if the cameras fail.[^hawkeye]

```{python}
#| label: fig-measure
#| fig-cap: "What changed in 2025, and what didn't. Left, the old way: the chain crew carries the sticks onto the field. At the start of the series an official clipped the chain at the nearest 5-yard stripe; laying that clip back on the same stripe puts the rear stick exactly where the series began, so the front stick, ten yards on, can be compared with the nose of the ball (the ball is drawn larger than scale). Right, a close-up of the same spot, about two yards across: since 2025, six cameras around the stadium measure the gap between the ball's nose and the line to gain, to a fraction of an inch. But in both, the ball sits where an official spotted it by eye (the shaded band is an illustrative margin of error, not a measured one): the cameras measure from that spot; they don't choose it."
q = Play([], None, los=62.0, ball_y="middle", to_go=None)   # d = yards past where this series began
LTG, NOSE = 10.0, 9.85                                     # line to gain; the ball's nose, about 5 inches short
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 4.0), gridspec_kw=dict(width_ratios=[1.25, 1]))


def ball_shape(ax, fld, w=0.0, scale=1.0):
    bx, by = XY(fld, q, NOSE - 0.155 * scale, w)
    ax.add_patch(Ellipse((bx, by), 0.19 * scale, 0.31 * scale, fc=style.BALL, ec="white", lw=0.6, zorder=9))


def ltg_line(ax, fld, w0, w1):
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = XY(fld, q, LTG, w0), XY(fld, q, LTG, w1)
    ax.plot([x0, x1], [y0, y1], color=style.LINE_TO_GAIN, lw=2.2, zorder=3)


# left: the chain crew's measurement on the field
ax = axes[0]
fld = Field(ax=ax, orient="vertical", los=69.0, window=(-8.0, 6.0), to_go=None,
            lateral=(MIDDLE - 6.5, MIDDLE + 6.5))
no_numbers(ax)
for ln in list(ax.lines):                       # the line of scrimmage Field draws is not part of this story
    if ln.get_color() == style.OFFENSE_DARK:
        ln.remove()
ltg_line(ax, fld, -6.5, 6.5)
ball_shape(ax, fld, scale=3.0)
for d_ in (0.0, LTG):
    ax.plot(*XY(fld, q, d_, 0.6), marker="s", ms=6, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, zorder=10)
ax.plot(*zip(XY(fld, q, 0.0, 0.6), XY(fld, q, LTG, 0.6)), color=style.INK_2, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (1, 1)), zorder=8)
ax.plot(*XY(fld, q, 3.0, 0.6), marker="D", ms=4.5, color=style.INK, zorder=10)
say(fld, q, 0.3, 3.2, "rear stick", fs=6.4)
say(fld, q, 3.0, 3.8, "clip laid on the\nnearest 5-yard\nstripe", fs=6.4)
say(fld, q, 11.0, 3.2, "front stick", fs=6.4)
say(fld, q, 10.9, -3.6, "line to gain", fs=6.4, color=style.INK)
say(fld, q, 8.0, -2.8, "the ball\n(not to scale)", fs=6.2, color=style.BALL, weight="bold")
ax.set_title("Until 2024: the chains walk out", fontsize=8.2, loc="left", fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
# right: a close-up of the same spot, where the cameras measure
ax = axes[1]
fld = Field(ax=ax, orient="vertical", los=62.0 + LTG, window=(-1.0, 0.9), to_go=None,
            lateral=(MIDDLE - 0.95, MIDDLE + 0.95), hashes=False, numbers=False)
xl, yl = ax.get_xlim(), ax.get_ylim()           # Field pads half a yard; at this zoom, drop the pad
ax.set_xlim(xl[0] + 0.5, xl[1] - 0.5); ax.set_ylim(yl[0] + 0.5, yl[1] - 0.5)
ltg_line(ax, fld, -0.95, 0.95)
band = [XY(fld, q, *pt) for pt in [(NOSE - 0.33, -0.95), (NOSE - 0.33, 0.95), (NOSE + 0.33, 0.95), (NOSE + 0.33, -0.95)]]
ax.add_patch(Polygon(band, closed=True, fc=style.DEFENSE, alpha=0.10, ec="none", zorder=2))
ball_shape(ax, fld)
(mx, my0), (_, my1) = XY(fld, q, NOSE, 0.28), XY(fld, q, LTG, 0.28)
ax.annotate("", xy=(mx, my1), xytext=(mx, my0), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=GREEN, lw=1.3,
                                                                 shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0), zorder=11)
say(fld, q, LTG + 0.5, 0.45, "measured: about\n5 inches short", fs=6.4, color=GREEN, weight="bold")
say(fld, q, LTG + 0.5, -0.5, "line to gain", fs=6.4, color=style.INK)
say(fld, q, NOSE - 0.62, 0.0, "the spot, chosen by eye\n(shaded: illustrative error)", fs=6.0,
    color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, weight="bold")
ax.set_title("Since 2025: cameras measure the gap", fontsize=8.2, loc="left", fontweight="bold",
             color=style.INK)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8)
plt.show()
```

The change is a nice lesson in two words that sound alike. *Precision* is how finely you can measure;
*accuracy* is whether you measured from the right place. The chains were not very precise (a clip laid by
hand, a chain pulled taut by eye), and they were slow. The cameras are extremely precise. But they measure
from the spot, and the spot is still a human judgment: an official running alongside the play, often
looking through a pile of bodies, deciding where the ball's nose was when forward progress stopped. A
measurement precise to a fraction of an inch, taken from a spot that could be off by a foot, is only as
accurate as the spot. That is why the spot itself can still be reviewed, but only in narrow cases: on a
play that's challenged or booth-reviewed, or through replay assist, the booth can move the spot when the
video clearly shows where the ball was relative to the line to gain or the goal line. (Who decides to
measure at all? The referee. A team's captain can ask him for one, but it's his call.)[^measure]

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"The cameras decide first downs now." They decide the *measurement*. The officials still spot the ball by
eye, and the yellow line on your screen is still the broadcaster's drawing, not an official mark. When a
spot looks wrong, the cameras can't help; only the replay booth's look at the spot can.
:::

## Reading the referee's announcement

Every announcement follows the same grammar, and once you know it you can usually finish the referee's
sentence for him. For a foul, the order is: **what** the foul was, **who** committed it (offense or defense,
and the player's number), **how much** it costs and **from where**, and **what happens to the down**.
For a review it's: the **outcome** (stands, confirmed, reversed), the **reason** in a sentence, and the
**result** (the new down, distance and spot, and anything about the clock).

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-announce
#| tbl-cap: "Six announcements decoded. The words in quotation marks are the typical form; referees vary the wording a little."
rows = [
    ("“Holding, number 72, offense. Ten-yard penalty. Repeat second down.”",
     "An accepted offensive holding foul: 10 yards from the previous spot, and the down is played again."),
    ("“Pass interference, defense, number 24. Spot foul. Automatic first down.”",
     "Defensive pass interference: the ball goes to the spot of the foul with a new set of downs."),
    ("“Offsetting fouls. Repeat third down.”", "A foul by each team; they cancel and the down is replayed."),
    ("“Illegal formation, offense. The penalty is declined. Fourth down.”",
     "The defense chose the play's result over the yards (a third-down incompletion, say)."),
    ("“After review, the ruling on the field stands. Third down.”",
     "The video wasn't clear enough to overturn the call, whichever way it was."),
    ("“After review, the ruling on the field is reversed. The runner's knee was down before the ball came out. "
     "There is no fumble. Second down.”",
     "The booth turned a turnover back into a tackle: the down-by-contact order of events."),
]
md_table(rows, ["What the referee says", "What it means"], [":--", ":--"])
```

The enforcement words in those sentences, *spot foul*, *declined*, *automatic first down* and the rest, are
taught in [Contact Rules and Penalties](09-03-contact-rules-and-penalties.qmd), which also explains when a
team should decline a penalty. Before the announcement, the referee's arm signal tells you most of it, and a
few signals cover most flags: a hand gripping the other wrist for holding; both hands on the hips for
offside or encroachment; forearms rolling over each other in front of the chest for a false start; both
open hands pushed forward from the shoulders for pass interference; one wrist chopping the other above the
head for a personal foul; and both arms, held parallel, waved diagonally across the body for intentional
grounding.[^signals]

### Do crews call games differently?

Each referee leads the same crew through a regular season, and fans and bettors love the idea that some
crews are "flag-happy". The data gives a measured answer. (The names are the referees who led each crew;
Shawn Hochuli, for one, is Ed Hochuli's son.)

```{python}
#| label: fig-crews
#| fig-cap: "Accepted penalties per game (both teams combined, every play) in games led by each referee's crew, 2024 (hollow) and 2025 (filled), for the referees who led a crew in both seasons, sorted by 2025. The grey band is the range around the 2025 league average that a crew would land in from game-to-game randomness alone, about two standard errors for a 16-game sample. Most crews sit inside it, and the order reshuffles from one season to the next. Source: nflverse play-by-play and officials data (regular seasons)."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.3))
ys = np.arange(len(wide))
ax.axvspan(avg25 - 2 * se_crew, avg25 + 2 * se_crew, color=style.GRID, alpha=0.7, lw=0, zorder=0)
ax.axvline(avg25, color=style.MUTED, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1)
for y, (name, row) in zip(ys, wide.iterrows()):
    ax.plot([row[2024], row[2025]], [y, y], color=style.BASELINE, lw=1.4, zorder=2)
    ax.plot(row[2024], y, "o", ms=6, mfc=style.SURFACE, mec=style.OFFENSE, mew=1.4, zorder=3)
    ax.plot(row[2025], y, "o", ms=6, color=style.OFFENSE, zorder=4)
ax.set_yticks(ys, wide.index, fontsize=7.2)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7)
ax.set_xlabel("Accepted penalties per game", fontsize=7.6)
ax.text(avg25, len(wide) - 0.2, f"2025 average {avg25:.1f}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=6.8,
        color=style.INK_2)
h = [Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", mfc=style.SURFACE, mec=style.OFFENSE, mew=1.4, ms=6, label="2024"),
     Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", color=style.OFFENSE, ms=6, label="2025")]
ax.legend(handles=h, loc="lower right", fontsize=7.2)
ax.set_ylim(-0.7, len(wide) + 0.4)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

In 2025 an average game had `{python} S["pen25"]` accepted penalties, and the crews' averages ran from
`{python} S["crew_lo"]` (`{python} S["crew_lo_name"]`'s crew) to `{python} S["crew_hi"]`
(`{python} S["crew_hi_name"]`'s).[^crewcalc] That spread sounds large until you set it against the noise. A
single game's total varies a lot (the standard deviation was about `{python} S["sd_game"]` penalties), so a
crew's 16- or 17-game average would wander about ±`{python} S["se2"]` around the league average by luck
alone. Most crews sit inside that band. And the ranking usually doesn't hold: the correlation between a
crew's 2024 and 2025 averages was `{python} S["r2425"]`, and across the ten seasons from 2016 to 2025 the
year-to-year correlation was usually weak (median `{python} S["r_med"]`), occasionally strong (it ranged
from `{python} S["r_lo"]` to `{python} S["r_hi"]`). Only `{python} S["same_half"]` of the `{python} S["ncrew"]` crews landed in the same
half of the table both years.

So crews differ a little, and inconsistently. Teams are hardly more predictable: a team's own rate of
accepted fouls has a median year-to-year correlation of `{python} S["team_r_med"]` over the same seasons.
Most of a single game's flag count, in other words, is noise: who happened to hold on which snap, in front
of which official. And some of the variation is the league's doing, not the crews': the league-wide average swings with points of
emphasis, from `{python} S["pen_lo"]` to `{python} S["pen_hi"]` per game across 2016–2025, which is why a
preseason memo telling officials to watch for a particular foul can move the numbers for every crew at once.

## Film room

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Cowboys at Packers, 2014 divisional playoffs, the catch that wasn't"}
Find the play: January 11, 2015, fourth quarter, 4:42 left, fourth-and-2 at the Green Bay 32, Dallas down
26–21. Watch Dez Bryant from the moment the ball arrives, and count the gates. Control: yes, he has it in
his hands above the cornerback. Feet: yes, he lands and takes steps. Time: here is the argument. He takes
three steps while falling and stretches the ball toward the goal line, and the ball hits the turf and moves
as he lands. Under the 2014 rule, he was going to the ground in the process of the catch, so his three
steps and his reach didn't count; he had to keep control through the ground, and replay ruled he hadn't.
Under the 2018 rule, those steps and that reach are acts common to the game, made before the ball touched
down, so the catch was complete before he landed. Watch the replay twice, once with each
rule in your head, and you'll understand why the league changed it.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Patriots at Jets, 2017, the touchback nobody recovered"}
October 15, 2017, fourth quarter, 8:31 left, the Jets down 24–14 at the New England 4. Austin
Seferian-Jenkins catches a short pass and turns toward the goal line; as he dives for it, with a defender
on him, the ball comes loose. Ruled a touchdown, it went to the booth as a scoring play. Replay ruled he lost the
ball before crossing the line and didn't regain control until he was already out of bounds in the end zone,
which made it a fumble out of the end zone. That second point was the argument afterward: two former
league officiating chiefs said on television they wouldn't have overturned it, and the league stood by the
call. Watch the referee's announcement: no defender recovered anything, and the Patriots got the ball at
their own 20. New England won by seven. Then watch the ball as he dives: anything held away from the body
near the goal line is exposed to exactly this outcome.[^asj]
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: the 2025 season, the cameras arrive"}
Pick any 2025 or 2026 game and wait for a close spot on third or fourth down. Watch the order of events: the
official spots the ball by eye, the referee signals for a measurement, and within about half a minute the
stadium screen shows the virtual line against the ball's nose. The chain crew never leaves the sideline. Then
watch the reactions: players and coaches now argue about the spot, the only human part left, and almost
never about the measurement.
:::

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it: the ref's mic"}
Every time a flag flies, or a ruling is close, make two calls before the referee turns on his microphone:

1. **Name the official.** Who threw it? A flag from the line of scrimmage at a sideline is the down or line
   judge (pre-snap foul, likely false start, offside or illegal formation). A flag from deep downfield is a
   side, field or back judge (likely pass interference or illegal contact). A flag from the backfield, near
   the quarterback, is the referee (roughing the passer, grounding) or the umpire (holding in the middle).
2. **Name the foul or the ruling**, and its result: how many yards, from where, and the down that follows.
3. **On every review, predict the outcome**: *reversed*, *confirmed* or *stands*. First ask who started it
   (a coach's flag, or the booth: after the two-minute warning, a score, a turnover). Then ask which angle would settle
   it. If the decisive moment is hidden (a pile, a body in the way), say *stands*.
4. **On every close catch, count the gates out loud**: control, feet, time.

Keep a tally for one game: officials named correctly, fouls named correctly, review outcomes called
correctly. You'll miss plenty at first; by the end of a season the official-then-foul habit will have you
announcing it before the referee does. Add your review predictions to
your prediction log.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: the sideline catch"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-sideline
#| fig-cap: "Second quarter, 1:52 left. The receiver (Z) catches a pass running toward the right sideline at the opponent's 38, gets his right foot down in bounds, then his left, and is knocked out of bounds by the cornerback. As he lands out of bounds the ball shifts in his hands, but his hands stay on it and it never touches the ground. The deep official on that side, about 20 yards downfield near the sideline (the far side from the chain crew), signals incomplete. The offense's head coach reaches for his red flag."
off = [O("QB", "QB", -6.5, -1.0, "Q"), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 13.0, "Z")]
dfn = [D("RCB", "CB", 15.0, 17.0, "C"), D("SS", "SS", 12.0, 7.0, "S")]
pp = Play(off, dfn, los=58, ball_y="right", to_go=6)
pp.route("Z", [(0, 0), (9.0, 0.5), (13.2, 8.8)], side=+1)
pp.path("RCB", [(13.3, 20.3)], absolute=True)                    # rallies down from deeper and drives him out
pp.pass_to("Z", t=1.6)
fld = pp.draw(lateral=(-3.0, 32.0), window=(-8.5, 22.5), title=False)
ax = fld.ax
no_numbers(ax)
official(ax, *XY(fld, pp, 19.6, 25.0), "FJ", fld.pts_per_yard(), r=1.3)
feet = [(12.6, 22.0), (14.0, 23.1)]                  # right foot, then left foot, both inside the line
for dd, ww in feet:
    ax.plot(*XY(fld, pp, dd, ww), marker="o", ms=5.5, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, zorder=11, mec="white", mew=0.6)
ball_at(fld, pp, 15.4, 25.6)
ax.annotate("", xy=XY(fld, pp, 12.3, 22.4), xytext=XY(fld, pp, 9.0, 25.0), zorder=11,
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=0.8))
say(fld, pp, 8.0, 26.6, "both feet down\nin bounds", fs=6.6, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, weight="bold")
say(fld, pp, 12.0, 28.4, "ball shifts\nin his hands\nas he lands", fs=6.4, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, weight="bold")
say(fld, pp, 3.0, 24.6, "sideline", fs=6.0, box=False, rot=90)
plt.show()
```

**Which official made the call? Can the coach challenge? Who decides, and what will the referee announce?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The field judge**: the deep wing official on the far side from the chain crew. **The coach can't
challenge**: the play came after the two-minute warning, so only the booth can review it, and a flag
would cost him a timeout for nothing. The replay official starts the review if he wants it (on a sideline
catch this close, he will), New York decides, and the referee announces.

The review runs the three gates. **Control**: secured before the ball touched anything? Yes. **Feet**:
right, then left, both in bounds with control? Yes. **Time**: a toe-tap along the sideline leaves no time
for a football act, so he had to **keep control through his landing out of bounds**. He did: a ball that
shifts in his hands while his hands stay on it is *slight movement*, not a loss of control, and it never
touched the ground. So: **"After review, the ruling on the field is reversed. The pass is complete."** The
ball is dead where he went out of bounds. No 10-second runoff, either: a catch that ends out of bounds stops
the clock anyway, so the correct ruling doesn't produce a running clock. (Had the ball come loose and hit
the ground as he landed, it would have been "the ruling on the field stands" or "is confirmed":
incomplete.)
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: reaching for the pylon"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-pylon
#| fig-cap: "Third-and-goal from the 3, third quarter, the offense in a heavy goal-line set (two tight ends, a fullback). The running back (R) bounces outside and dives for the pylon, holding the ball out in his outside arm. At the 1 the cornerback (C), coming from outside, punches it loose; it bounces into the end zone and rolls out of bounds through the side of the end zone. Nobody touches it after the punch."
gl = [O(k, k, -0.7, w, "") for k, w in [("LT", -3.2), ("LG", -1.6), ("C", 0.0), ("RG", 1.6), ("RT", 3.2)]]
gl += [O("YL", "TE", -0.7, -4.8, "Y"), O("YR", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 17.0, "Z"),
       O("QB", "QB", -2.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("FB", "FB", -4.4, 0.0, "F"), O("RB", "RB", -6.8, 0.0, "R")]
pz = Play(gl, [D("SS", "SS", 3.5, 8.0, "S"), D("CB", "CB", 3.0, 20.5, "C")], los=107, ball_y="right", to_go=None)
pz.run("RB", [(-3.2, 4.0), (-1.6, 9.6), (2.0, 14.2)], absolute=True)       # bounces outside the tight end
pz.path("SS", [(2.6, 11.2)], absolute=True)
pz.path("CB", [(1.2, 15.8)], absolute=True)
fld = pz.draw(lateral=(-8.5, 30.0), window=(-8.5, 13.5), title=False)
ax = fld.ax
no_numbers(ax)
xmark(fld, pz, 2.0, 14.2)
path_arrow(fld, pz, [(2.0, 14.2), (4.8, 17.6), (7.5, 23.58), (8.0, 24.8)])
say(fld, pz, -2.5, 25.2, "sideline", fs=6.0, box=False, rot=90)
say(fld, pz, 3.6, 4.0, "goal line", fs=6.2)
say(fld, pz, 11.8, 12.0, "end line", fs=6.2)
say(fld, pz, -5.0, 19.8, "punched out\nat the 1", fs=6.6, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, weight="bold")
say(fld, pz, 8.6, 17.0, "out of bounds\nin the end zone", fs=6.6, color=style.BALL, weight="bold")
plt.show()
```

**What's the ruling, and who gets the ball where? What if the ball had gone out of bounds at the 1 instead?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A fumble through the end zone: touchback.** The ball was fumbled forward into the opponent's end zone and
went out of bounds there, so the defense takes over at its own 20, even though it never recovered the ball.
Because it's a turnover (and was close to a score), the booth reviews it automatically, in order. First:
**did the ball break the plane of the goal line, or touch the pylon, while he still had it?** If so, it's a
touchdown and nothing after matters. Second: was he down before the ball came out? Only if he'd been
touched and his knee or body hit the ground first, in which case it's fourth-and-goal from the 1. Third:
did the loose ball really go out in the end zone? (A loose ball that hits the pylon counts as out of bounds
there too: touchback.)

If the ball had gone out of bounds *at the 1*, short of the goal line, the offense would keep it. And
because a fumble that goes out forward comes back to the spot of the fumble, it would be at the 1, where the
punch knocked it out: fourth-and-goal. The difference between those two outcomes is a few feet of turf and
several points of [expected points](../13-analytics-and-data/13-02-expected-points-and-success-rate.qmd),
which is why coaches tell runners to carry the ball high and tight near the goal line instead of reaching
for the pylon.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: flushed and thrown away"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-grounding
#| fig-cap: "Third-and-8 at the offense's own 30. The quarterback is flushed from the pocket to his right, well outside the tackle box (shaded), with the end closing on him and his receivers covered downfield. Running toward the sideline, he throws the ball away; it lands out of bounds a yard short of the line of scrimmage. A flag flies from the backfield. The referee (R) is shown where he started the play, behind the quarterback on his throwing-arm side."
gg = [O(k, k, -0.7, w, "") for k, w in [("LT", -3.2), ("LG", -1.6), ("C", 0.0), ("RG", 1.6), ("RT", 3.2)]]
gg += [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -4.6, -2.6, "R")]
pg = Play(gg, [D("DE", "DE", -1.0, 5.0, "E"), D("DT", "DT", -1.0, -2.0, "T")], los=40, to_go=8)
pg.path("QB", [(-7.5, 1.0), (-8.0, 7.0), (-7.0, 12.5)], absolute=True)
pg.block("RB", pts=[(0.8, -0.8)])
fld = pg.draw(lateral=(-12.0, 30.5), window=(-14.0, 6.0), title=False)
ax = fld.ax
no_numbers(ax)
tackle_box(ax, fld, pg, -14.0)
official(ax, *XY(fld, pg, -11.5, 5.5), "R", fld.pts_per_yard(), r=1.15)
path_arrow(fld, pg, [(-1.0, 5.0), (-4.6, 7.4), (-6.0, 10.6)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.4, ls="-", head=10)  # the end closes
path_arrow(fld, pg, [(-7.0, 12.5), (-1.0, 27.8)], color=style.BALL, lw=1.6)
ball_at(fld, pg, -1.0, 27.8)
say(fld, pg, -9.0, 22.0, "lands out of bounds,\na yard short of the line", fs=6.4, color=style.BALL, weight="bold")
say(fld, pg, -11.8, -4.8, "tackle box", color=PURPLE, fs=6.4, weight="bold")
say(fld, pg, 1.4, -7.0, "line of scrimmage", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fs=6.2)
say(fld, pg, 1.0, 25.4, "sideline", fs=6.0, box=False, rot=90)
plt.show()
```

**Who threw the flag, and for what? Where is the ball, and what down is it?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The referee, for intentional grounding.** He's the official who watches the quarterback, and grounding is
his call. Run the conditions. *Pressure*: the end was closing, so a sack was coming. *No receiver near*: the
ball landed out of bounds with nobody around it. *The box*: he was outside it, so the exception applies,
**but only if the ball reaches the line of scrimmage**, and this one landed a yard short. That's grounding.
(Had it landed a yard past the line, out of bounds, it would have been a legal throwaway.)

The penalty: **loss of down and 10 yards** from the previous spot, because the spot of the pass (about 7
yards behind the line) is less than 10 yards back. The ball goes from the 30 back to the 20, and the lost
down means it's **fourth-and-18**: almost certainly a punt. The referee will announce: *"Intentional
grounding, offense. Ten-yard penalty and loss of down. Fourth down."* Replay
assist can't help him: it may wipe out a grounding flag only when the passer was outside the pocket, and
being outside isn't what made this one grounding.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **Seven officials split the field and the players.** The referee (white cap) watches the quarterback and
  announces; the umpire watches the interior line; the down and line judges own the line of scrimmage and the
  sidelines; the side, field and back judges own the receivers downfield. Where a flag came from tells you
  what it is likely to be.
- **Replay has three doors, and the order of questions matters.** Is the ruling reviewable at all (judgment
  fouls aren't)? Is it one the booth reviews automatically (scores, tries, turnovers, short on fourth down,
  anything after the two-minute warning or in overtime)? If not, only a coach's challenge, paid for with a
  timeout, can open it. Replay assist runs alongside all three on clear objective facts and, since 2024, the
  objective part of a short list of flags. There is no sky judge.
- **Reversals need clear and obvious evidence**, so a hidden moment usually "stands", and "stands" and
  "confirmed" leave the play exactly as called.
- **A catch is three gates: control, feet down, then time.** Since 2018 a football act made on the way down
  finishes the catch; only a receiver who hits the ground before he's had time for one must survive the
  ground. The rule now matches what people see, at the price of a judgment about time.
- **The order of events decides possession, and direction and territory decide the rest.** Ball out before
  the knee is a fumble; an NFL runner needs to be touched to be down. A forward fumble out of bounds comes back
  to the spot of the fumble, but into the opponent's end zone and out it's a touchback. A pass that doesn't go
  forward is a backward pass and stays live if dropped. Grounding is about the box and the line: once outside
  the box, a throwaway just has to reach the line.
- **Cameras measure, people spot**, and crew differences in flags are small and unstable from year to year.

## Connections

**Builds on:** [Contact Rules and Penalties](09-03-contact-rules-and-penalties.qmd) (the fouls these
officials call, and how they are enforced: spot fouls, accept or decline, half the distance) and
[Quarterback Play](../04-the-passing-game/04-07-quarterback-play.qmd) (the throwaway, and why a quarterback
leaves the pocket). The spot, forward progress and the chain crew were introduced in
[Downs, Distance, and Field Position](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd); the
end zone and the plane of the goal line in
[The Game in Fifteen Minutes](../01-foundations/01-01-the-game-in-fifteen-minutes.qmd); the touchback on
kicks in [Field Goals, Extra Points, and the Punting Game](09-01-kicking-and-punting.qmd); the challenge
decision and the staff who advise on it in
[What a Play Really Is](../01-foundations/01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd); and why tempo offenses hurry
to beat a challenge in
[In-Game Adjustments and Tempo](../08-the-chess-match/08-04-in-game-adjustments-and-tempo.qmd).

**Sets up:** [The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd),
where spikes, grounding, the booth's control of the final two minutes and the value of a timeout spent on a
challenge all become clock decisions; and
[Red Zone, Goal Line, Two-Point Plays, and Short Yardage](../10-situational-football/10-03-red-zone-goal-line-and-short-yardage.qmd),
where forward progress and the goal-line spot decide the tush push and every fourth-and-inches. The rules'
history (the 1978 passing changes, the catch rule, replay) is placed in context in
[The 1978 Liberation](../11-history/11-02-the-1978-liberation.qmd) and Appendix E, and Part 13 shows how to
pull the review and penalty data behind this chapter's charts yourself
([nflverse in Python](../13-analytics-and-data/13-01-nflverse-in-python.qmd)).

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper"}
- The **NFL Rulebook** (NFL Football Operations, free online): Rule 3 (definitions, including the catch and
  the pocket area), Rule 7 (dead ball, down by contact), Rule 8 (forward and backward passes, intentional
  grounding, fumbles), Rule 11 (touchbacks) and Rule 15 (instant replay). The league also publishes
  officiating videos explaining recent rulings, with the same angles the replay officials use.
- **Football Zebras** (footballzebras.com), written by former officials and longtime followers of
  officiating: crew assignments, rule changes and play-by-play explanations of controversial calls.
- **nflverse** (via `nflreadpy`): `load_officials()` for every game's crew since 2015 and the play-by-play
  `desc` text for every recorded review and penalty, enough to rebuild both charts in this chapter and test
  your own theories about crews.
- Former NFL officiating chiefs (Mike Pereira, Dean Blandino) explain controversial calls on broadcasts and
  in columns every week; following them is the fastest way to learn how the people in the booth think.
:::

[^crew]: The positions and duties follow the NFL's own descriptions ("Officials' responsibilities and
    positions," NFL Football Operations), as reproduced in Crescent City Sports, "Breakdown of duties for NFL
    game officials" (Oct. 20, 2019): referee and umpire 10–12 yards deep in the backfield, side judge and field
    judge 20 yards downfield, back judge 25 yards:
    <https://crescentcitysports.com/breakdown-of-duties-for-nfl-game-officials/> ; "Official (American
    football)," Wikipedia, for the referee favoring the quarterback's throwing arm and the seven abbreviations:
    <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official_(American_football)>.

[^umpire]: The umpire was moved to the offensive backfield for the 2010 season after a run of injuries to
    umpires in the middle of the defense (five serious ones in 2009). Because walking up from the backfield
    to spot the ball slowed hurry-up offenses, from 2010 to 2015 he returned to the defensive side in the
    closing minutes of the game (Wikipedia gives the last five minutes; some accounts of the 2010 rule add
    the last two minutes of the first half); that exception was dropped in 2016, and since 2023 he works on
    the defensive side on field goals and extra points. "Official (American football),"
    Wikipedia (umpire): <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official_(American_football)>.

[^officials]: Part-time status and the full-time experiments of 2017, 2019 and 2020: Associated Press,
    "NFL set to begin hiring and training replacement officials, AP sources say" (Mar. 30, 2026), via WTOP:
    <https://wtop.com/nfl/2026/03/nfl-set-to-begin-hiring-and-training-replacement-officials-ap-sources-say/> .
    Playoff crews assembled from individually graded officials ("mixed crews"; all-star crews only for the
    conference championships and the Super Bowl): Ben Austro, "How does the NFL assign mixed crews for the
    playoffs," Football Zebras (Jan. 6, 2025):
    <https://www.footballzebras.com/2025/01/how-does-the-nfl-assign-mixed-crews-for-the-playoffs-2024/> . The
    one-year contingency rule: Fox News, "2026 NFL rule changes: 1-year rule to allow replay center to correct
    mistakes approved" (Mar. 31, 2026):
    <https://www.foxnews.com/sports/2026-nfl-rule-changes-1-year-rule-allow-replay-center-correct-mistakes-approved> .
    The seven-year agreement (May 8, 2026, through 2032): Pro Football Rumors, "NFL, NFLRA agree to seven-year
    CBA": <https://www.profootballrumors.com/2026/05/nfl-nflra-agree-to-seven-year-cba>.

[^seventh]: The NFL went to seven officials in 1978 by adding the side judge; the back judge and field judge
    exchanged titles in 1998 to match college and high-school usage; and the head linesman was renamed the
    down judge in 2017. "Official (American football)," Wikipedia (history):
    <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official_(American_football)> ; "1998 NFL season," Wikipedia:
    <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_NFL_season>. The 1978 changes to pass-defense rules are

[^challenges]: NFL Rulebook (2026), Rule 15, Section 1: two challenges, each needing an available timeout;

[^reviewcalc]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play, 2016–2025: plays flagged `replay_or_challenge`,
    classified by their description ("[team] challenged the ... ruling" for a coach's challenge, "The Replay
    Official reviewed the ... ruling" for the booth) and by the result ("REVERSED" or "Upheld"; nflverse text
    does not separate "stands" from "confirmed"). Challenge figures are regular season only. Reviews that ended
    quickly without a stoppage are generally not written into the play text.

[^catchrule]: NFL Rulebook (2026), Rule 8, Section 1, Article 3 (completed or intercepted pass): control in
    the hands or arms before the ball touches the ground; both feet or another body part other than the hands
    in bounds; then an act common to the game, or control long enough to perform one; Note 1, movement of the
    ball does not automatically mean loss of control; Note 2, a player who has not yet made the act and loses
    control when he hits the ground, in bounds or out, has not caught it; Note 4, a simultaneous catch by two
    eligible opponents belongs to the passing team, but not if one player had control first: <https://operations.nfl.com/rules-officiating/2026-nfl-rulebook>.

[^catchnew]: NFL.com, "NFL teams unanimously approve simplified catch rule" (Mar. 27, 2018; control, two feet
    or another body part down, and a football move such as a third step or reaching for the line, or the
    ability to perform one; the going-to-the-ground element removed):
    <https://www.nfl.com/news/story/0ap3000000923342/article/nfl-teams-unanimously-approve-simplified-catch-rule> ;
    CBS Sports, "NFL catch rule: Dez Bryant, Jesse James non-catches would now count" (Troy Vincent and Al

[^downrule]: NFL Rulebook (2026), Rule 7, Section 2, Article 1(a) (the ball is dead when a runner is contacted

    (a runner who slides or gives himself up) and 1(b) (the ball is dead when a runner's forward progress ends,
    so a runner then pushed out of bounds is treated as down in bounds): <https://operations.nfl.com/rules-officiating/2026-nfl-rulebook> ; NCAA Football Rules, Rule 4-1-3 (a ball carrier is down
    when any part of his body other than a hand or foot touches the ground, contact or not).

    wrist striking the other above the head; intentional grounding: parallel arms waved in a diagonal plane
    across the body): <https://operations.nfl.com/rules-officiating/2026-nfl-rulebook>.

[^crewcalc]: Course calculation, 2024 and 2025 regular seasons: nflverse `load_officials()` (the referee of each
    game) joined to play-by-play; accepted fouls counted from the play text, where nflverse writes an accepted
    foul as "PENALTY on" and a declined or offsetting one as "Penalty on". Both teams' fouls on every play,
    including kicks and pre-snap fouls, are counted. The band uses the 2025 game-level standard deviation and the
    average number of games per crew. Year-to-year correlations use every referee who led a crew in consecutive
    seasons, 2016–2025; the team version counts each team's accepted fouls from the same play text, divided by
    16 games a season through 2020 and 17 from 2021. Ed and Shawn Hochuli: "Ed Hochuli," Wikipedia:
    <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Hochuli>.
